meta.title: Why Energy May Be the Best Investment of the Next Decade with Wil VanLoh
meta.speakers: Wil VanLoh (founder, Quantum Capital Group), with Christopher Zook and Mark Wade (CAZ Investments); intro by Tony Robbins
meta.thread_line: 6 threads · capital exodus · peak shale and a 9% reserve-replacement alarm · OPEC power and $100 oil · power-grid squeeze and build-baby-build · data science as edge · grit and capital allocators

snapshot: Wil VanLoh, founder of Quantum Capital Group, argues oil, gas and midstream have the **best risk-adjusted returns of any major asset class** today.
Over 80% of private equity capital in the space is gone since pre-COVID; the private sector has only 10-20% of what it needs.
Global reserve replacement has fallen to **9%** over the last five years versus 200%+ from WWII to the '90s — a $3.5-4T underinvestment deficit.
US shale, which supplied ~100% of global oil supply growth for 15 years, peaks "very soon"; pricing power shifts back to OPEC, whose breakeven is $90-95 vs ~$67-68 oil.
Inflation-adjusted, oil "should be" triple digits and US gas ~$10/MMBtu, not $3 — highly inflationary, and the end of energy subsidizing every other sector.
US power demand, flat for 15 years, is projected up ~20% in five years; turbines take 5+ years and new gas plants cost up to $2.5M/MW, so existing plants trade below replacement cost.
Quantum's edge is data: the largest driller in North America (~65 rigs), with data science now its biggest single discipline.
Hosts are investors in Quantum; a closing segment covers leadership traits and grit.

themes.status: OVER 80% OF SECTOR PE CAPITAL GONE SINCE PRE-COVID
themes.title: A capital-starved sector that looks like the mid-1990s — with the best risk-adjusted returns anywhere
themes.lead: Capital fled oil and gas on poor returns and ESG just as demand fundamentals turned the best they've ever been.
bullets: VanLoh: oil, gas and midstream have the best risk-adjusted returns of any major asset class globally — he sees nothing better from his family office.
Over **80%** of private equity available to the space five to six years ago is gone — poor returns plus ESG.
Quantum lost **every European institutional investor** in its last fundraise (closed last fall); its European ultra-high-net-worth families mostly doubled or tripled.
In the US a third to 40% of LPs leaned in; the 2021-23 wait-and-see LPs are now actively looking, a swing that took off after Trump's election.
Private companies drove over half the shale boom but now have 10-20% of the capital they need; public equity goes to buybacks and distributions, not growth.
Demand drivers: billions of people climbing the economic ladder plus AI as a "massive massive consumer of energy."
Echo of the mid-'80s-to-mid-'90s bust, when **90%** of companies went out of business and the survivors had real competitive advantage.

quote.text: It's got the best riskadjusted returns uh of any major asset class globally.

themes.title: Peak shale and a 9% reserve-replacement alarm: a $3.5-4T hole
themes.lead: A decade of underinvestment shows up as the lowest reserve replacement on record, and shale can no longer bail the world out.
bullets: Global cycle time from first exploration dollar to first production is **7-8 years**; shale is the exception.
US shale revolution "is going to peak very soon" and no other shale revolution is expected globally — back to slow conventional assets.
Underinvestment of **$350-400B a year** since 2014 has built a $3.5-4T global deficit.
Reserve replacement: 200%+ from WWII to the '90s; below 100% in the '90s (lowest decade ~60%); above 100% in the 2000s; below in the 2010s; **9%** in the last five years.
Zook: the ~60% decade was followed by **$140 crude**.
Too much capital rushing in? "We are nowhere close" — VanLoh doesn't see it as an issue for a very long time.
Shale tech (horizontal drilling plus hydraulic fracturing) took the US from most energy-dependent to most energy-independent country in ~20 years.

quote.text: The last five years, it's been 9%. Okay. Anybody that understands this stuff should be alarmed.

themes.title: Pricing power shifts back to OPEC — oil "should be" triple digits, gas $10
themes.lead: With US shale no longer supplying all global growth, OPEC+ regains pricing power, and its budgets need far higher prices.
bullets: Over 15 years the US delivered almost **100%** of global oil supply growth, tripled oil output, more than doubled gas, and now produces ~22% of global supply.
OPEC pumps ~30M of a ~100M barrel/day market and Russia ~10M; Saudi, UAE and Russia run their governments off oil revenue.
OPEC breakeven without tapping sovereign funds is **$90-95/barrel** versus ~$67-68 today — and they want more to refill the coffers.
Housing, food, healthcare and education are up 60-80% over 15 years while oil fell by half and gas ~75%.
Inflation-adjusted, oil could be triple digits and US gas ~$10/MMBtu (the global price) vs a ~$3 five-year average.
Cheap energy "basically subsidized every other sector"; that ending is inflationary, matters for S&P valuations and has geopolitical consequences.
Zook: energy build-out is inflationary any way you slice it — one reason CAZ is in the **higher-for-longer** rates camp.

quote.text: It's basically subsidized every other sector allowed those sectors to raise their prices while its prices have come down and and that is coming to an end.

themes.status: BOUGHT 11 GAS PLANTS BELOW 50 CENTS ON THE DOLLAR
themes.title: Power demand wakes up after 15 flat years — build-baby-build makes existing plants worth more
themes.lead: Data-center demand meets an old grid, slow courts and a hollowed-out turbine supply chain, so existing assets trade far below what new ones cost.
bullets: US power demand grew just 0.2-0.3%/year for 15 years (1-2% before); projected **~20%** growth over the next five years, ~2.5-3%/year.
Antiquated transmission, little new build, and more wind/solar make the grid less stable; battery storage adds cost.
Williams CEO Alan Armstrong at CERAWeek: **$2 on regulatory for every $1** spent putting pipe in the ground.
A GE or Siemens gas turbine takes five years minimum; US turbine manufacturing capacity is down ~75% since the early-2000s build-out, with global back orders.
New gas plants cost ~$1.7-1.8M per MW (up to $2.5M) vs ~$1M before — "build baby build" strains supply chains and is inflationary.
Quantum bought **Cogentrix** (11 gas-fired plants) earlier this year for about $3B, under 50 cents on the dollar of replacement cost.
Nuclear is "the absolute best answer"; tech and society are getting behind it, and Quantum is building nuclear capability.

quote.text: There's no drill baby drill or, you know, we need to be building baby build.

themes.status: DATA SCIENCE IS QUANTUM'S BIGGEST DISCIPLINE
themes.title: Machine learning on frac knobs: proprietary drilling data as the investing edge
themes.lead: Shale has dozens of tunable variables, and a firm with clean proprietary data can price risk — and dodge bad deals — better than one using public data.
bullets: ML is "statistics on steroids"; shale has many knobs — lateral landing, sand, water, pump rate, stages, clusters per stage — so the payoff is large.
Industry is in the first or beginning of the second inning of applying AI at scale; VanLoh says he has still "meaningfully underestimated" its impact.

Quantum (founded at VanLoh's age 28) staffed engineers, geologists and geophysicists beside investors from day one, borrowing the Silicon Valley VC model; it started collecting digital data a decade-plus before peers.
Its portfolio is the **largest driller in North America**, ~65 rigs or 12-13% of US rigs running.

Public data is dirty (production allocated by algorithm); proprietary data cleans it. Hired Chevron's global digital architect; ~15 of a 75-person investment team are data staff, plus 30-40 full-time contractors in India.

ROI is tracked directly (cost saved, revenue added), but the bigger value is separating **bad rock from bad operators**, spotting juiced production, and walking away from deals that could lose hundreds of millions.
Generalists who chased the first shale decade mostly lost; "five or six" specialists survived by identifying, pricing and managing risk.

themes.status: WHAT QUANTUM LOOKS FOR IN LEADERS
themes.title: Integrity, downside focus, lifelong learning and grit — "80% of the battle"
themes.lead: VanLoh backs people for integrity, proven capital allocation with a downside focus, creative lifelong learning, and grit.
bullets: Origin: small-town central Texas, a football injury at TCU, a value-investing course from a Graham & Dodd disciple, then Kidder Peabody's energy group.
Started Windrock (energy capital-raising and M&A) just before 24 and Quantum at 28 — once had investors rent his car because he was under 25.
Traits: integrity and win-win; **proven capital allocators** who obsess over the downside; lifelong learners who hold views loosely; grit to get up after plans get "ripped up."
Adversity forged him most in 54 years; Zook (golf walk-on, trading commodities through school) cites Tony Robbins' "life is happening for you."
Wade: energy is physical — real commodities and property; "success is a horrible teacher."
~300 CAZ investors toured the energy floor at the Houston Museum of Natural Science; Zook's 92-year-old mother-in-law spent five hours on ChatGPT.

takeaways.title: Treat oil and gas underinvestment as a multi-year setup, not a trade — cycles run 7-8 years.
Hedge portfolios for energy-led inflation if oil heads toward OPEC breakeven.
Favor existing generation and pipeline assets over new build while turbines take five years.
Back energy managers with in-house technical and data teams, not generalists.
Judge leaders on downside discipline and learning speed, not past wins.

other_news.title: Europe: Russia-Ukraine sent energy costs soaring, and the continent now faces rearming at hundreds of billions to a trillion euros a year; its ESG-driven retreat from hydrocarbons was "much more pronounced" than the US.
No energy form has been replaced in 180 years — the world uses more of every kind than ever; Quantum stays all-of-the-above (oil, gas, midstream, wind, solar, storage, building nuclear).
Sources referenced: Alan Armstrong (Williams) at CERAWeek; Ben Graham and David Dodd's value-investing tradition; Tony Robbins.
